prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock, credited to Katori and Ye. The chair's summary shows that the committee is choosing between two single parts, B022 and B012, and the question is which one is the stronger discovery or invention today, not which is more fashionable. The lattice clock is one identifiable idea, trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the lattice perturbs both clock levels equally and Doppler and recoil shifts vanish, followed by a demonstrated step to the 10^-18 regime through ultrastable lasers and systematic control. Its performance has been confirmed in independent laboratories and species for years, so there is no maturity doubt, and the 2005 prize concerned the frequency comb, a different enabling tool. It has changed what can be tested: gravitational redshift over millimetre scales, constraints on varying constants, relativistic geodesy. I would word the citation around the lattice-clock architecture and its 10^-18 realisation so that ion-clock, comb and ultrastable-laser contributors are not implicitly demoted, which answers the chair's fifth question. I treat the pending redefinition of the second as supporting evidence of impact and not as a criterion, which answers the sixth.
statement.case_against: The credit for B012 is a two-name line drawn through a broad community: Al+ and Yb+ ion-clock groups, SYRTE, PTB, NIST and the JILA team members around Ye, and Hall and Haensch for the comb, are all outside the pair. Priority of the magic-wavelength proposal over contemporaneous proposals has not been verified in the material before us, and I should not claim it has. It is also an invention in precision measurement and not a new phenomenon, and some colleagues will read that as less far-reaching than a new class of quantum matter. B022 is scientifically spectacular, and my concern is not its merit but that its experimental credit (Dean, the first author of the 2018 papers, Young, Yacoby, Efetov, Yazdani) is wider than the three names and that the superconducting mechanism is open after eight years. I do not see a fair two-part split of B022 and B012 inside three people, so I do not propose one.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B022 as a single part but cautions that the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gives flat bands and does not by itself predict the correlated phases, and he concedes that waiting would settle interpretation and credit.
responses.response: Your caution about the theory credit moves me toward being firmer, not softer. If the citation cannot claim that theory predicted the correlated insulators and superconductivity, then the theory names and the experimental name are credited for two different things, and the experimental side is still wider than Jarillo-Herrero. That is a real attribution cost that I do not see for the lattice clock, where the concept and the precision realisation sit with two named people. I also accept your concession that waiting a few years would help B022, and that is my reason for ranking it as alternative and not first. I would support a restricted wording of the B022 citation in a later year, but I do not think it removes the credit problem today.

responses.point: Mehlig values B022 as the cleanest theory-to-experiment story, with one geometric knob giving access to Mott-like and superconducting physics, and he treats the unsettled pairing mechanism as an interpretation question separate from the secure discovery.
responses.response: I agree that the existence of flat bands, correlated insulators and superconducting domes is secure and reproduced, and I do not use the unresolved mechanism to dispute the discovery itself. My disagreement is narrower: you also acknowledge that the first-author student, hBN-encapsulated device work and later groups are outside the names, and you accept a real attribution cost. For me that cost, together with the age of the field, is enough to rank B022 second, whereas you rank B012 eighth for pending societal impact. I do not think that pending impact is the right test, because the lattice clock's impact is already demonstrated in comparisons, redshift measurements and bounds on constants. We differ on whether a measurement invention is a discovery of the same kind, and I think a result that changes what can be tested qualifies.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a real, tunable regime of quantum matter and that the theory-plus-experiment split maps naturally onto the three supplied names.
responses.response: The field-opening impact is real, and in round 1 I overstated the contrast by saying the superconductivity is unresolved as if it undermined the discovery; it does not. Where the three-name mapping is concerned, I now think it is less natural than it first appears, given Eriksson's point that the continuum model does not predict the correlated phases and the chair's question about the authorship of the 2018 papers. I have not seen that author record in the material before me and would want it checked before a final vote. If it showed that Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero clearly cover the core credit, I would move B022 up as my first alternative and could accept it, but I would not rank it above B012 on the present record.

responses.point: Lindroth treats B012 as a single well-defined invention and concedes that the ion-clock groups, SYRTE, PTB and JILA team members are broader than two names, and that she may be underweighting the pull of a large new field.
responses.response: I agree with your attribution concern, and I think it is addressed by wording rather than by adding names: the citation should name the lattice-clock architecture and its 10^-18 realisation, so that no one reads it as ranking lattice clocks above ion clocks. On your underweighting worry, I considered it and did not change my preferred configuration, because the breadth of a new field is a reason to wait for its credit to become clear and not a reason to prefer it to a cleanly attributed result now. I also share your caution on the second: I would not make the prize depend on the redefinition.

uncertainties: Whether priority for the magic-wavelength proposal over contemporaneous proposals has been checked; the committee papers do not settle it.
Whether the author and credit record of the 2018 B022 papers would support a three-name allocation; I have not seen it, and a clear result could move B022 above my alternative.
Whether the committee will accept that a precision-measurement invention is a prize-level result of the same kind as a new quantum phase.
How the pending redefinition of the second should weigh; I treat it as supporting evidence only.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye belongs to the JILA precision-measurement community around Hall, so there is a loose lineage connection with B012 that I disclose for the committee to judge; I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye and no connection to any B022 name. My earlier flag of rare-earth-ion quantum-memory work concerned B054, which is not on the shortlist, so no recusal is needed on any shortlisted ballot. I will abide by the chair's guidance if the committee wants me to recuse on B012.
